questions.questionText: Your enterprise has a strict mandate to exit its colocation data center within 90 days due to an expiring lease. The environment consists of 800 VMware vSphere virtual machines with highly interdependent, undocumented legacy applications, complex Layer 2 multicast networking topologies, and rigid static IP dependencies. The business requires minimal disruption and cannot tolerate any code refactoring during this phase. Which workload disposition strategy and architecture should you implement?
options: Replatform the workloads by containerizing them using Migrate to Containers and deploying them to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to achieve cloud-native efficiencies.
Rehost the workloads to Google Cloud VMware Engine (GCVE), utilizing HCX to stretch Layer 2 networks and perform vMotion migrations without altering IP addresses.
Refactor the legacy applications into microservices using Cloud Run to completely eliminate the technical debt of the undocumented virtual machines.
Rehost the workloads to Google Compute Engine using Migrate to Virtual Machines, mapping the legacy Layer 2 multicast networks to isolated VPC subnets.
correctAnswers: Rehost the workloads to Google Cloud VMware Engine (GCVE), utilizing HCX to stretch Layer 2 networks and perform vMotion migrations without altering IP addresses.

explanation.general explanation: A 'Rehost' (Lift and Shift) strategy using Google Cloud VMware Engine (GCVE) is the only viable solution to meet the aggressive 90-day timeline for 800 highly interdependent VMs. GCVE natively supports VMware HCX, which allows for Layer 2 network stretching and live vMotion migrations, completely preserving the IP addresses and complex L2 topologies (like multicast) without requiring any application changes or downtime.

why other options are wrong.Replatform the workloads by containerizi: Replatforming 800 undocumented, interdependent legacy applications to containers within 90 days is highly risky and almost impossible. It also violates the requirement to avoid code/architecture refactoring.
why other options are wrong.Refactor the legacy applications into mi: Refactoring is a multi-year effort that directly violates the prompt's constraints of a 90-day deadline and the prohibition against code refactoring.
why other options are wrong.Rehost the workloads to Google Compute E: While GCE is a valid Rehost target, Google Cloud VPCs do not natively support Layer 2 multicast traffic or seamless L2 stretching without complex overlay networks. This would break the complex legacy networking requirements.

questions.questionText: A financial institution runs a core banking monolith on an on-premises mainframe. The application handles millions of transactions daily with deep dependencies on proprietary IBM Db2 features. The C-suite wants to migrate to Google Cloud to reduce licensing costs but insists on an iterative disposition strategy that mitigates risk. They want to modernize the architecture gradually over 3 years rather than attempting a big-bang migration. Which disposition strategy should you advocate for?
options: A Repurchasing strategy, replacing the custom mainframe application immediately with a SaaS core banking product to eliminate all technical debt.
A Rehosting strategy using a mainframe emulator on Google Compute Engine to lift-and-shift the entire stack in one weekend, followed by optimization.

A Strangler Fig Refactoring strategy, deploying an API gateway in front of the mainframe and gradually rewriting specific business domains into microservices on Google Cloud while routing legacy calls to the mainframe.
A Replatforming strategy, using the Database Migration Service to copy the Db2 data to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, and recompiling the COBOL code to run on App Engine.
correctAnswers: A Strangler Fig Refactoring strategy, deploying an API gateway in front of the mainframe and gradually rewriting specific business domains into microservices on Google Cloud while routing legacy calls to the mainframe.

explanation.general explanation: The Strangler Fig pattern is the definitive architectural strategy for gradually modernizing (Refactoring) monolithic systems while mitigating risk. By placing an API gateway (like Apigee) in front of the monolith, you can intercept client requests. You then build new microservices in Google Cloud for specific business domains (e.g., 'Account Balance'). The gateway routes 'Account Balance' requests to the new cloud service and all other requests back to the legacy mainframe, slowly 'strangling' the legacy system over the 3-year timeline.

why other options are wrong.A Repurchasing strategy, replacing the c: While Repurchasing is a valid disposition, doing it 'immediately' violates the C-suite's explicit requirement for an iterative, risk-mitigated 3-year transition.
why other options are wrong.A Rehosting strategy using a mainframe e: A 'big-bang' weekend migration of a core banking mainframe is incredibly high risk and directly contradicts the business requirement to avoid a big-bang migration.
why other options are wrong.A Replatforming strategy, using the Data: You cannot simply recompile COBOL to run natively on App Engine Standard. Furthermore, Db2 proprietary features often do not translate 1:1 to PostgreSQL without significant refactoring, making this an unviable Replatforming approach.

questions.questionText: Your organization uses a highly customized, internally developed Customer Relationship Management (CRM) system deployed on bare-metal servers. The system provides absolutely no competitive advantage, costs millions annually in maintenance, and requires a dedicated team of 20 developers just to keep it running. The business wants to redirect these engineering resources to revenue-generating machine learning projects. What is the most appropriate workload disposition strategy for this CRM system?
options: Replatform the CRM system to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to reduce infrastructure management overhead.
Refactor the CRM system into serverless functions using Cloud Run and Cloud Functions to minimize compute costs.
Repurchase (Drop and Shop) by migrating the CRM data to a managed SaaS solution like Salesforce or HubSpot, and decommission the legacy system.
Retain the CRM system on-premises but implement Cloud Interconnect to allow the new machine learning models in Google Cloud to query its database.
correctAnswers: Repurchase (Drop and Shop) by migrating the CRM data to a managed SaaS solution like Salesforce or HubSpot, and decommission the legacy system.

explanation.general explanation: The 'Repurchase' (or Drop and Shop) disposition strategy involves abandoning a legacy application and moving to a commercial Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) alternative. This is the perfect strategy for workloads that provide no competitive differentiation (like standard CRMs or HR systems) but consume massive amounts of operational and developer resources. Moving to SaaS frees the 20 developers to work on core, revenue-generating business initiatives.

why other options are wrong.Replatform the CRM system to Google Kube: Replatforming only changes the infrastructure layer. The 20 developers would still be required to maintain the complex, custom CRM application code, failing to meet the business goal.
why other options are wrong.Refactor the CRM system into serverless: Refactoring a massive custom CRM would require an enormous initial investment of developer time, exactly the opposite of the goal to redirect engineering resources immediately to ML projects.
why other options are wrong.Retain the CRM system on-premises but im: Retaining the workload means the business continues to pay millions in maintenance and the 20 developers remain trapped supporting legacy code.

questions.questionText: Your team is evaluating the disposition of a large-scale, on-premises Apache Hadoop cluster used for nightly batch processing. The cluster runs 24/7, but compute utilization is only above 10% during the 4-hour nightly batch window. The data engineering team does not have the capacity to rewrite the complex MapReduce and Spark jobs into a new framework. The business mandates a massive reduction in Total Cost of Ownership (TCO). How should you architect the migration?
options: Rehost the Hadoop cluster by deploying standard Compute Engine VMs, installing Hadoop manually, and purchasing 3-year Committed Use Discounts to lower the TCO.
Refactor the batch processes by rewriting the MapReduce jobs as serverless Cloud Dataflow pipelines to achieve a pay-per-use billing model.
Replatform the workload by migrating the Hadoop jobs to Cloud Dataproc. Configure ephemeral Dataproc clusters via Workflow Templates that spin up, execute the jobs, and terminate immediately after.
Repurchase a third-party managed analytics platform from the Google Cloud Marketplace to handle the nightly batch jobs natively.
correctAnswers: Replatform the workload by migrating the Hadoop jobs to Cloud Dataproc. Configure ephemeral Dataproc clusters via Workflow Templates that spin up, execute the jobs, and terminate immediately after.

explanation.general explanation: Replatforming to Cloud Dataproc using ephemeral clusters is the optimal strategy. Dataproc is Google's managed Hadoop/Spark service. By moving to Dataproc, the team avoids rewriting the complex jobs (satisfying the constraint). Transitioning from a persistent 24/7 on-prem cluster to an ephemeral cluster that only runs for the 4-hour batch window drastically reduces TCO, as you only pay for compute exactly when it is actively processing data.

why other options are wrong.Rehost the Hadoop cluster by deploying s: While CUDs lower costs, running a cluster 24/7 when it is only utilized for 4 hours is a massive waste of resources and an anti-pattern for cloud data processing. TCO reduction is minimal compared to ephemeral models.
why other options are wrong.Refactor the batch processes by rewritin: The prompt explicitly states: 'The data engineering team does not have the capacity to rewrite the complex MapReduce and Spark jobs'. Refactoring is out of scope.
why other options are wrong.Repurchase a third-party managed analyti: Repurchasing requires abandoning the existing MapReduce/Spark codebase, which implies entirely rebuilding the logic in the new platform. This violates the lack of engineering capacity.

questions.questionText: You are leading a cloud migration assessment for a healthcare company (similar to EHR Healthcare). They have a critical, monolithic patient records database running on Oracle RAC (Real Application Clusters) on specialized on-premises hardware. The database utilizes extensive proprietary PL/SQL procedures and requires sub-millisecond latency to the physical storage layer. The licensing agreement prohibits running this specific Oracle database in a virtualized multi-tenant cloud environment. The business wants to exit their local data center but cannot afford the multi-year risk of migrating off Oracle. Which disposition strategy is required?
options: Refactor the database schema to Google Cloud Spanner to achieve global consistency and 99.999% availability.
Replatform the database to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL using the Database Migration Service (DMS) to translate the PL/SQL procedures automatically.
Rehost the Oracle RAC environment onto Google Cloud Bare Metal Solution (BMS) to comply with licensing and hardware latency requirements.
Retain the database on-premises and connect it to Google Cloud compute resources using a Dedicated Interconnect.
correctAnswers: Rehost the Oracle RAC environment onto Google Cloud Bare Metal Solution (BMS) to comply with licensing and hardware latency requirements.

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud Bare Metal Solution (BMS) is specifically designed to Rehost specialized, hardware-dependent workloads like Oracle RAC. Because the licensing prohibits virtualized environments, and the workload requires specialized hardware for sub-millisecond storage latency, BMS provides dedicated, physical servers located in a regional extension connected directly to the Google Cloud backbone. This allows the customer to exit their data center, maintain their Oracle licenses, and avoid the massive risk of refactoring.

why other options are wrong.Refactor the database schema to Google C: The business explicitly 'cannot afford the multi-year risk of migrating off Oracle'. Refactoring to Spanner is a massive, multi-year undertaking.
why other options are wrong.Replatform the database to Cloud SQL for: While DMS helps migrate data, 'extensive proprietary PL/SQL' rarely translates automatically with 100% accuracy. This still represents a high-risk refactoring effort that the business rejected.
why other options are wrong.Retain the database on-premises and conn: The prompt states 'The business wants to exit their local data center'. Retaining it on-premises violates this core business objective.

questions.questionText: Your company is migrating a large, monolithic e-commerce application from an on-premises data center to Google Cloud using the Strangler Fig pattern. You have containerized the legacy monolith and deployed it to a GKE cluster. You are now building new microservices (e.g., 'Inventory', 'Checkout') in Cloud Run. You need to architect the traffic routing layer to securely and dynamically route API requests between the legacy monolith and the new microservices based on URL paths. Which two actions should you take to implement this disposition architecture? (Choose two)
options: Deploy an External Application Load Balancer as the primary ingress point.
Deploy Cloud DNS and create A records to load balance traffic evenly across GKE and Cloud Run.
Configure URL Maps on the Load Balancer to route `/api/inventory` to a Serverless Network Endpoint Group (NEG) pointing to Cloud Run.
Implement VPC Network Peering between the GKE cluster and the Cloud Run instances to route traffic internally.
Configure the Load Balancer to use TCP Proxy to inspect the HTTP headers and route traffic accordingly.
correctAnswers: Deploy an External Application Load Balancer as the primary ingress point.
Configure URL Maps on the Load Balancer to route `/api/inventory` to a Serverless Network Endpoint Group (NEG) pointing to Cloud Run.

explanation.general explanation: To implement the Strangler Fig pattern at the network edge, you require an intelligent Layer 7 proxy capable of inspecting HTTP requests and routing them to different backends. The External Application Load Balancer serves as this global ingress point. You then use URL Maps to define the routing logic. For example, legacy traffic (`/*`) routes to a Zonal NEG (GKE), while modernized endpoints (`/api/inventory/*`) are intercepted and routed to a Serverless NEG (Cloud Run). This allows seamless, transparent migration of capabilities.

why other options are wrong.Deploy Cloud DNS and create A records to: DNS cannot route traffic based on HTTP URL paths (like `/api/inventory`). It only resolves hostnames to IPs. Furthermore, evenly balancing traffic between legacy and new services would break application logic.
why other options are wrong.Implement VPC Network Peering between th: VPC Peering connects networks; it does not perform Layer 7 HTTP request routing based on paths, which is the core mechanism of the Strangler pattern from the client's perspective.
why other options are wrong.Configure the Load Balancer to use TCP P: A TCP Proxy operates at Layer 4 and cannot inspect HTTP headers or URL paths. An Application Load Balancer (Layer 7) is required.

questions.questionText: An enterprise organization relies on a fleet of 50 Windows Server 2008 R2 virtual machines hosting a legacy, proprietary 32-bit line-of-business application. The original vendor went bankrupt 10 years ago, and the source code is lost. The application is highly sensitive to latency and requires direct block storage access. The organization must evacuate their data center. Standard Google Compute Engine does not support 32-bit operating systems or Windows Server 2008 R2. Which workload disposition strategy is technically viable for this specific workload?
options: Refactor the application by decompiling the 32-bit binaries and recompiling them to a 64-bit architecture compatible with Cloud Run.
Replatform the application using Migrate to Containers to automatically extract the application state and run it in a Windows container on GKE.
Rehost the workload onto Google Cloud VMware Engine (GCVE), as vSphere natively supports legacy 32-bit operating systems and Windows Server 2008.
Retain the workload on-premises, as Google Cloud provides zero solutions for legacy 32-bit Windows applications.
correctAnswers: Rehost the workload onto Google Cloud VMware Engine (GCVE), as vSphere natively supports legacy 32-bit operating systems and Windows Server 2008.

explanation.general explanation: When dealing with extreme legacy OS constraints (32-bit architectures, unsupported legacy Windows versions) where source code is missing, Rehosting via Google Cloud VMware Engine (GCVE) is the standard escape hatch. GCVE runs native VMware vSphere, which maintains deep backward compatibility with legacy operating systems that standard cloud hypervisors (like Compute Engine) have long since deprecated. This allows the organization to evacuate the data center without modifying the unsupported OS.

why other options are wrong.Refactor the application by decompiling: Decompiling proprietary binaries without source code to refactor an architecture is practically impossible, highly error-prone, and often legally perilous.
why other options are wrong.Replatform the application using Migrate: Windows Server containers require modern OS versions (Windows Server 2019+). You cannot run a 32-bit Windows 2008 application in a modern GKE Windows container.
why other options are wrong.Retain the workload on-premises, as Goog: This is incorrect because GCVE provides a fully supported environment within Google Cloud data centers for these legacy vSphere workloads.

questions.questionText: Your team is defining the workload disposition strategy for a tightly coupled, monolithic e-commerce application. The business requires the application to scale dynamically during Black Friday sales and wants to transition to a microservices architecture. However, they only have 6 months before the next Black Friday event, which is not enough time to rewrite the massive codebase. They want to maximize scalability now, with a plan to refactor later. Which migration path should you choose?
options: Rehost (Lift and Shift) the monolith to standard Compute Engine VMs, as this is the only strategy that can be completed in 6 months.
Repurchase a SaaS e-commerce platform and migrate the user data, abandoning the custom monolith entirely before Black Friday.
Replatform (Lift and Optimize) the monolith by containerizing the application 'as-is' and deploying it to a GKE Autopilot cluster to enable horizontal pod autoscaling.
Refactor the application aggressively by breaking the database into multiple Cloud SQL instances, even if the code rewrite takes 8 months.
correctAnswers: Replatform (Lift and Optimize) the monolith by containerizing the application 'as-is' and deploying it to a GKE Autopilot cluster to enable horizontal pod autoscaling.

explanation.general explanation: Replatforming (Lift and Optimize) represents the ideal middle-ground when time is constrained but cloud-native benefits (like autoscaling) are required. By containerizing the monolith 'as-is' (without rewriting the underlying code), the team can meet the 6-month deadline. Deploying it to GKE allows them to leverage Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA) to handle the Black Friday traffic spikes, establishing a solid foundation for future, iterative refactoring into microservices.

why other options are wrong.Rehost (Lift and Shift) the monolith to: While Rehosting is fast, traditional VM autoscaling is slower and more cumbersome than container autoscaling. Containerizing a monolith is completely feasible within 6 months and provides vastly superior scaling benefits.
why other options are wrong.Repurchase a SaaS e-commerce platform an: Moving an entire custom e-commerce business process to a SaaS platform within 6 months right before Black Friday is extremely high risk and disrupts core business operations.
why other options are wrong.Refactor the application aggressively by: The prompt explicitly states the deadline is 6 months. A strategy that takes 8 months is invalid.

questions.questionText: During a migration discovery phase using Google Cloud Migration Center, you identify a cluster of 15 virtual machines running an open-source message broker (RabbitMQ) that facilitates asynchronous communication between legacy applications. The VMs are underutilized, but the operations team spends 20 hours a week patching the OS, managing the cluster quorum, and dealing with split-brain scenarios. The development team is willing to update the application client libraries. What is the most operationally efficient workload disposition strategy?
options: Rehost the RabbitMQ VMs directly to Compute Engine to minimize disruption to the legacy applications.
Replatform the RabbitMQ workload by migrating the VMs to Google Cloud VMware Engine (GCVE).
Refactor the architecture by replacing the self-managed RabbitMQ cluster with Google Cloud Pub/Sub, updating the application code to publish and subscribe to Pub/Sub topics.
Retire the asynchronous messaging system and refactor the applications to communicate via synchronous REST APIs to eliminate the message broker overhead.
correctAnswers: Refactor the architecture by replacing the self-managed RabbitMQ cluster with Google Cloud Pub/Sub, updating the application code to publish and subscribe to Pub/Sub topics.

explanation.general explanation: Replacing self-managed infrastructure software (like RabbitMQ or Kafka) with a fully managed, serverless Google Cloud service (like Pub/Sub) is a textbook Refactoring (or Rearchitecting) disposition. Because the prompt states the operations team wastes 20 hours a week maintaining the VMs and quorum, and the developers are willing to update the client libraries, moving to Pub/Sub entirely eliminates the operational overhead (NoOps), scaling seamlessly while handling asynchronous communication.

why other options are wrong.Rehost the RabbitMQ VMs directly to Comp: Rehosting simply shifts the operational burden (OS patching, cluster quorum management) from the on-prem data center to Google Cloud. It does not solve the 20-hour/week operational inefficiency.
why other options are wrong.Replatform the RabbitMQ workload by migr: GCVE abstracts the hypervisor, but the operations team still has to manage the guest OS and the RabbitMQ application layer, solving none of the operational pain points.
why other options are wrong.Retire the asynchronous messaging system: Switching from asynchronous to synchronous communication fundamentally changes the application's resilience and temporal decoupling, likely introducing massive performance and availability risks.

questions.questionText: Your organization is defining disposition strategies for its global portfolio. You encounter a specialized inventory application deployed in a manufacturing plant in Germany. The application controls high-speed robotics on the assembly line, requiring a guaranteed response time of less than 3 milliseconds. Furthermore, German works council regulations dictate that the robotic control telemetry data must never leave the physical boundaries of the facility. However, the corporate IT team insists on managing this application's container lifecycle using the same Google Cloud control plane they use for their global GKE fleet. Which strategy satisfies all constraints?
options: Retain the workload locally by deploying Google Distributed Cloud (Anthos on bare metal) within the German facility to process data locally while managing it via the Google Cloud Console.
Refactor the application to use Cloud IoT Core and process the telemetry streams using Cloud Dataflow in the `europe-west3` (Frankfurt) region to ensure low latency.
Rehost the application to a dedicated Compute Engine sole-tenant node in the `europe-west3` region to ensure physical hardware isolation for the telemetry data.
Replatform the application to Cloud Run in the `europe-west3` region, utilizing VPC Service Controls to prevent the telemetry data from being exfiltrated outside of Germany.
correctAnswers: Retain the workload locally by deploying Google Distributed Cloud (Anthos on bare metal) within the German facility to process data locally while managing it via the Google Cloud Console.

explanation.general explanation: This scenario defines a strict 'Retain' (Hybrid/Edge) disposition constraint due to physics (< 3ms latency to local robots is impossible if routed to a remote cloud region) and strict data residency (telemetry cannot leave the facility). Google Distributed Cloud (formerly Anthos on bare metal or GDC Edge) allows you to run Kubernetes clusters on your own hardware inside the factory. This keeps the data processing local (meeting latency and data residency) while projecting the cluster into the Google Cloud control plane for centralized lifecycle management.

why other options are wrong.Refactor the application to use Cloud Io: Routing traffic from the factory floor to Frankfurt and back will exceed the 3ms latency requirement. Furthermore, sending the telemetry to GCP violates the strict data residency requirement.
why other options are wrong.Rehost the application to a dedicated Co: Moving the workload to GCP Frankfurt violates the data residency constraint ('must never leave the physical boundaries of the facility') and the latency constraint.
why other options are wrong.Replatform the application to Cloud Run: VPC Service Controls protect GCP APIs, but the data has still left the physical facility and travelled to Google's data center, violating the core compliance constraint.

questions.questionText: You are assisting a media company with their workload disposition planning. They have a massive on-premises data archive containing 15 PB of historical video footage stored on an aging Storage Area Network (SAN). The legacy video editing software running on nearby workstations mounts this SAN via NFS and cannot be modified or updated. The business wants to decommission the expensive SAN hardware but must maintain the ability for the workstations to access the files via NFS. What is the correct Replatforming strategy?
options: Migrate the 15 PB of data to Cloud Storage using Storage Transfer Service, and update the workstations to use the Cloud Storage JSON API.
Deploy an array of Google Cloud Filestore High Scale instances, migrate the data, and establish a Cloud VPN to mount the Filestore shares directly to the on-prem workstations.
Migrate the data to Cloud Storage using Storage Transfer Service, and deploy Cloud Storage FUSE on the on-premises workstations to mount the buckets as local file systems.
Migrate the 15 PB of data to Cloud Storage. Deploy an Edge Cache appliance or a third-party hybrid cloud storage gateway on-premises that exposes an NFS endpoint back to the workstations.
correctAnswers: Migrate the 15 PB of data to Cloud Storage. Deploy an Edge Cache appliance or a third-party hybrid cloud storage gateway on-premises that exposes an NFS endpoint back to the workstations.

explanation.general explanation: When replatforming massive unstructured data sets (15 PB) where the legacy client cannot be altered and requires standard POSIX/NFS access, Cloud Storage is the only cost-effective scalable backend. However, because the workstations are on-premises and need low-latency NFS mounts, deploying a hybrid cloud storage gateway (or Edge Cache) locally is the standard architectural pattern. The gateway exposes a standard NFS mount to the legacy software, caches active files locally for performance, and asynchronously tiers the 15 PB of cold data back to inexpensive Cloud Storage.

why other options are wrong.Migrate the 15 PB of data to Cloud Stora: The prompt explicitly states the legacy video editing software 'cannot be modified or updated'. You cannot force it to use a REST API.
why other options are wrong.Deploy an array of Google Cloud Filestor: Storing 15 PB of historical archive data on Filestore High Scale is astronomically expensive. Filestore is meant for high-performance compute workloads, not massive, cold video archives.
why other options are wrong.Migrate the data to Cloud Storage using: Cloud Storage FUSE does not provide full POSIX compliance, and running it directly over a WAN (from on-prem to GCP) for video editing will result in terrible latency and performance bottlenecks. A local caching gateway is required.

questions.questionText: An insurance company relies on a custom-built, monolithic policy rating engine written in Java. The application is stateless, currently deployed on dozens of bare-metal servers, and experiences highly unpredictable traffic spikes, occasionally overwhelming the physical hardware. The company wants to modernize the architecture to achieve infinite, hands-off scalability while minimizing the amount of code they need to rewrite. Which workload disposition strategy provides the best balance of modernization and effort?
options: Rehost the application onto a Compute Engine Managed Instance Group with autoscaling enabled based on CPU utilization.
Refactor the Java application entirely into hundreds of independent Cloud Functions to achieve true serverless execution.
Replatform the application by containerizing the Java monolith using Google Cloud Buildpacks and deploying it to Cloud Run.
Repurchase a third-party managed rating engine from a SaaS provider and migrate the actuarial algorithms.
correctAnswers: Replatform the application by containerizing the Java monolith using Google Cloud Buildpacks and deploying it to Cloud Run.

explanation.general explanation: The application is already stateless, which makes it a perfect candidate for containerization. Using Google Cloud Buildpacks allows the team to containerize the Java application with almost zero code changes (minimizing effort). Deploying this container to Cloud Run (a fully managed serverless platform) provides the 'infinite, hands-off scalability' required for unpredictable traffic spikes. This perfectly defines a Replatforming (Lift and Optimize) strategy.

why other options are wrong.Rehost the application onto a Compute En: While Rehosting to a MIG provides autoscaling, VM scaling is relatively slow (taking minutes to boot) compared to Cloud Run's near-instantaneous scaling. It also leaves the team managing OS patching, which is not 'hands-off'.
why other options are wrong.Refactor the Java application entirely i: Refactoring a monolith into hundreds of functions requires massive code rewrites and architectural redesign, violating the business requirement to 'minimize the amount of code they need to rewrite'.
why other options are wrong.Repurchase a third-party managed rating: Rating engines are often the core intellectual property of an insurance company. Repurchasing forces them to abandon their custom actuarial logic, which is highly undesirable.

questions.questionText: Your team has assessed a portfolio of 500 legacy applications for cloud migration. You categorize 50 applications as 'Retire'. These applications are ancient internal tools that the IT department believes are no longer used by the business. However, blindly shutting them down carries significant risk if a critical quarterly financial process still depends on them. What is the safest architectural approach to executing the 'Retire' disposition strategy for these workloads?
options: Deploy Google Cloud Network Intelligence Center on-premises to map network dependencies.
Perform a 'Scream Test' by permanently deleting the virtual machines and waiting to see if business users complain.
Implement fine-grained VPC Flow Logs in the on-premises network to monitor active inbound connections to the application servers over a 90-day period.
Use StratoZone or Migration Center dependency mapping agents to observe inbound and outbound process-level traffic over a full business cycle.
Migrate the applications to preemptible VMs in Google Cloud so they terminate randomly, revealing hidden dependencies safely.
correctAnswers: Implement fine-grained VPC Flow Logs in the on-premises network to monitor active inbound connections to the application servers over a 90-day period.
Use StratoZone or Migration Center dependency mapping agents to observe inbound and outbound process-level traffic over a full business cycle.

explanation.general explanation: Executing a 'Retire' strategy safely requires empirical proof that an application is truly dead. Relying on human knowledge is flawed. The best architectural approach is data-driven dependency mapping. Using Google Cloud Migration Center agents (or StratoZone) provides deep, process-level network dependency mapping. Alternatively, analyzing network flow logs over a full business cycle (e.g., 90 days to catch quarterly reporting jobs) definitively proves whether any downstream systems or users are still communicating with the servers before they are decommissioned.

why other options are wrong.Deploy Google Cloud Network Intelligence: Network Intelligence Center is a Google Cloud-native tool used for analyzing traffic within GCP VPCs. It cannot be deployed on-premises to map legacy networks.
why other options are wrong.Perform a 'Scream Test' by permanently d: A 'scream test' is an amateur, high-risk operational anti-pattern. If a critical quarterly financial process fails because the server was deleted, the business impact could be catastrophic.
why other options are wrong.Migrate the applications to preemptible: Migrating applications just to let them fail randomly is a massive waste of migration effort and introduces unpredictable chaos, entirely failing the goal of a safe retirement.

questions.questionText: A healthcare provider is planning the disposition of its core Electronic Health Records (EHR) database. The database is currently a massive, single-node PostgreSQL instance on-premises. The business requires the cloud architecture to provide a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) of zero and a Recovery Time Objective (RTO) of less than 60 seconds across multiple geographic regions to protect against localized disasters. Which disposition strategy and target architecture should you choose?
options: Replatform to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL configured for Cross-Region High Availability.
Refactor the application schema to use Cloud Spanner in a Multi-region configuration.
Rehost to a Compute Engine custom VM using a persistent disk (pd-ssd) replicated asynchronously to a secondary region.
Replatform to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, utilizing the continuous backup and point-in-time recovery features.
correctAnswers: Refactor the application schema to use Cloud Spanner in a Multi-region configuration.

explanation.general explanation: An RPO of zero (no data loss) and RTO of < 60 seconds across *multiple geographic regions* is an incredibly stringent requirement. Cloud Spanner is Google Cloud's globally distributed, strongly consistent relational database. A Multi-region Spanner instance synchronously replicates data across regions, natively providing an RPO of 0 and near-zero RTO during a regional failure. While this requires Refactoring the application to use Spanner's specific schema and transaction paradigms, it is the only architecture that meets the absolute physics of the business requirement.

why other options are wrong.Replatform to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL c: Cloud SQL Cross-Region Replicas use *asynchronous* replication. In the event of a primary region failure, asynchronous replication guarantees data loss (RPO > 0), violating the strict RPO 0 requirement.
why other options are wrong.Rehost to a Compute Engine custom VM usi: Asynchronous disk replication inherently implies an RPO > 0 (some data is lost in transit during a hard failure). It also requires manual failover, likely exceeding the 60-second RTO.
why other options are wrong.Replatform to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, ut: Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) relies on restoring from backups and transaction logs. Restoring a massive database takes significantly longer than 60 seconds, severely violating the RTO requirement.

questions.questionText: Your company is executing a 'Replatform' disposition strategy for its portfolio of legacy Java EE (J2EE) applications running on Oracle WebLogic. The applications are highly stateful, storing HTTP session data directly in the application server memory. The business wants to containerize these applications and deploy them to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to standardize operations. What crucial architectural modification must you implement during this replatforming effort to ensure the applications scale correctly in GKE?
options: Configure the GKE Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) to scale based on Memory utilization rather than CPU utilization.
Implement session affinity (sticky sessions) on the Google Cloud Ingress controller to ensure user requests always hit the same GKE Pod.
Externalize the HTTP session state by configuring the applications to store session data in a managed Memorystore (Redis) instance.
Deploy the WebLogic containers using a StatefulSet instead of a Deployment to guarantee stable network identifiers.
correctAnswers: Externalize the HTTP session state by configuring the applications to store session data in a managed Memorystore (Redis) instance.

explanation.general explanation: While Replatforming typically minimizes code changes, moving a highly stateful application to a distributed, ephemeral environment like GKE requires addressing state. If session data is kept in local Pod memory, scaling down (or Pod eviction) destroys active user sessions. Scaling up means new Pods don't have the session data. The architectural best practice is to externalize state to a fast, centralized, in-memory datastore like Memorystore for Redis. This makes the GKE Pods truly stateless and safe to auto-scale dynamically.

why other options are wrong.Implement session affinity (sticky sessi: Sticky sessions are a band-aid, not a solution for cloud-native scaling. If a node fails or the cluster scales down, the Pod dies, and all 'stuck' user sessions are permanently lost, causing a severe degradation in user experience.
why other options are wrong.Configure the GKE Horizontal Pod Autosca: Scaling based on memory does not solve the fundamental architectural flaw of storing state in ephemeral, distributed compute nodes.
why other options are wrong.Deploy the WebLogic containers using a S: StatefulSets provide stable network identities and persistent storage for databases (like running Cassandra in K8s). They do not magically synchronize in-memory HTTP session state across multiple application replicas.

questions.questionText: Your retail company uses an on-premises data warehouse built on Microsoft SQL Server. The marketing team runs complex analytical queries (OLAP) that frequently take 12 hours to complete, causing reports to be delivered a day late. The data engineering team wants to execute a Refactoring strategy to modernize the data architecture in Google Cloud, aiming for near real-time analytics. They want to move away from managing index fragmentation and relational schema constraints. Which target architecture should they choose?
options: Migrate the data to Cloud SQL for SQL Server to offload database maintenance, utilizing read replicas for the analytical queries.
Migrate the data to Cloud Spanner, utilizing its distributed architecture to accelerate the complex OLAP queries.
Migrate the data warehouse to BigQuery, utilizing its columnar storage and serverless execution engine to drastically reduce query times.
Migrate the database to Compute Engine VMs using the newest generation of AMD EPYC processors and NVMe SSDs.
correctAnswers: Migrate the data warehouse to BigQuery, utilizing its columnar storage and serverless execution engine to drastically reduce query times.

explanation.general explanation: Moving an analytical (OLAP) data warehouse from a traditional relational database (like SQL Server) to a modern, cloud-native Enterprise Data Warehouse (EDW) like BigQuery is the ultimate Refactoring strategy for analytics. BigQuery's columnar storage architecture and massive parallel processing engine are specifically designed to execute complex analytical queries across massive datasets in seconds or minutes, resolving the 12-hour query problem without the need to manage indexes or relational constraints.

why other options are wrong.Migrate the data to Cloud SQL for SQL Se: This is a Replatforming strategy. While it offloads maintenance, Cloud SQL is an OLTP database. It will struggle with the same massive 12-hour OLAP queries because the underlying relational architecture remains the same.
why other options are wrong.Migrate the data to Cloud Spanner, utili: Cloud Spanner is designed for massive, globally consistent OLTP (transactional) workloads. While it can handle some analytics, BigQuery is the dedicated, vastly superior, and cheaper tool for pure OLAP data warehousing.
why other options are wrong.Migrate the database to Compute Engine V: This is a Rehosting (Lift and Shift) strategy. Throwing faster hardware at a fundamentally inefficient relational OLAP architecture is a costly band-aid, not a modernization strategy.

questions.questionText: The Mountkirk Games case study highlights their desire to replace their monolithic backend, which currently runs on bare-metal servers. They want to move to a fully managed, globally scalable environment to support rapid global expansion and massive traffic spikes. They are willing to rewrite the application code to achieve this. Which workload disposition strategy and target GCP architecture perfectly aligns with Mountkirk Games' business objectives?
options: Replatform the monolithic backend by packaging it into containers and deploying it to a global fleet of GKE clusters.
Rehost the monolithic backend to Compute Engine Managed Instance Groups across multiple regions, utilizing Global Load Balancing.
Refactor the backend into microservices managed by Google Kubernetes Engine, and utilize Cloud Spanner as the global database.
Repurchase a third-party managed gaming backend SaaS to eliminate the need for internal developers to write code.
correctAnswers: Refactor the backend into microservices managed by Google Kubernetes Engine, and utilize Cloud Spanner as the global database.

explanation.general explanation: In the Mountkirk Games case study, the explicit technical requirement is to move away from their existing legacy bare-metal environment and 'replace their monolithic backend' with an architecture that can 'scale globally' and handle massive multiplayer game state. Refactoring into microservices on GKE provides the compute scalability, and pairing it with Cloud Spanner perfectly addresses their requirement for a globally scalable, strongly consistent database to store player profiles and game state.

why other options are wrong.Replatform the monolithic backend by pac: While containerizing helps, simply replatforming a monolith does not address the fundamental database scaling issues or the explicit desire to 'replace their monolithic backend' with a modern architecture.
why other options are wrong.Rehost the monolithic backend to Compute: Rehosting retains the technical debt of the monolith and does not leverage the advanced, managed, scalable services required by the case study's business vision.
why other options are wrong.Repurchase a third-party managed gaming: Mountkirk Games explicitly states they want to 'build their new game backend on Google Cloud'. They are a game development company; repurchasing their core intellectual property is counter to their business model.

questions.questionText: Your team is executing a massive Rehosting (Lift and Shift) migration from an on-premises VMware environment to Google Compute Engine using Migrate to Virtual Machines. You have mapped the legacy networks to a new Google Cloud Shared VPC. During a pilot migration of a complex multi-tier application, the application boots successfully in Google Cloud but fails to communicate with its database, which is still running on-premises pending a later migration wave. What architectural component is missing from your disposition strategy?
options: You must configure Cloud DNS forwarding zones in the Google Cloud VPC to resolve the on-premises database hostnames.
You must implement an HA VPN or Cloud Interconnect to establish a hybrid network connection between the Google Cloud VPC and the on-premises network.
You must assign an External IP address to the Google Cloud VM so it can reach the on-premises database over the internet.
You must install the Migrate to Virtual Machines agent on the on-premises database server to enable cross-environment communication.
correctAnswers: You must implement an HA VPN or Cloud Interconnect to establish a hybrid network connection between the Google Cloud VPC and the on-premises network.

explanation.general explanation: In a phased Rehosting migration, applications are moved in 'waves'. This frequently results in a split-stack architecture (e.g., app tier in GCP, database tier on-prem). To allow the newly migrated VMs in the Google Cloud VPC to securely communicate with the remaining on-premises resources using private RFC 1918 IP addresses, a hybrid connectivity solution (HA VPN or Cloud Interconnect) is an absolute mandatory prerequisite.

why other options are wrong.You must configure Cloud DNS forwarding: While DNS forwarding is necessary for name resolution, resolving the name is useless if there is no physical network route (VPN/Interconnect) to transport the IP packets back to the on-premises network.
why other options are wrong.You must assign an External IP address t: Exposing internal enterprise database traffic over the public internet is a massive security violation and an architectural anti-pattern.
why other options are wrong.You must install the Migrate to Virtual: The Migrate to VMs agent is used to orchestrate the storage replication and migration process. It does not act as a network router or proxy for application traffic.

questions.questionText: Your company is running a legacy Active Directory (AD) Domain Services environment on-premises. As part of your workload disposition strategy, you are moving all file servers, print servers, and employee identity management to Google Workspace (a Repurchase strategy). However, you have 5 legacy applications being Rehosted to Compute Engine that still rely heavily on LDAP and Kerberos authentication against Active Directory. What is the most operationally efficient disposition strategy for the Active Directory workload itself?
options: Retire Active Directory completely. Refactor the 5 legacy applications to use SAML 2.0 and authenticate directly against Google Cloud Identity.

Replatform Active Directory by adopting Google Cloud Managed Service for Microsoft Active Directory (Managed Microsoft AD) and establishing a trust relationship with the remaining on-prem AD during transition.
Rehost the Active Directory domain controllers to standard Compute Engine VMs, ensuring you configure static IPs and manage the Windows Server patching manually.
Repurchase identity management by moving entirely to Google Workspace and utilizing Google Secure LDAP to authenticate the legacy Windows VMs.
correctAnswers: Replatform Active Directory by adopting Google Cloud Managed Service for Microsoft Active Directory (Managed Microsoft AD) and establishing a trust relationship with the remaining on-prem AD during transition.

explanation.general explanation: Because the 5 legacy applications are being Rehosted (not Refactored) and strictly require LDAP/Kerberos, you must maintain an Active Directory environment. The most operationally efficient (NoOps) strategy is to Replatform to Google Cloud Managed Microsoft AD. This provides a highly available, Google-managed actual Microsoft AD domain, eliminating the operational overhead of patching and securing domain controller VMs, while natively supporting the required legacy protocols.

why other options are wrong.Retire Active Directory completely. Refa: The prompt states the applications are being 'Rehosted', implying a lack of desire or ability to rewrite the code. Refactoring legacy apps to support modern SAML/OIDC is often complex or impossible without source code.
why other options are wrong.Rehost the Active Directory domain contr: While possible, Rehosting AD onto IaaS VMs requires the customer to manually manage the OS, patching, and high availability, which is significantly less operationally efficient than the managed service.
why other options are wrong.Repurchase identity management by moving: Google Secure LDAP provides LDAP authentication, but it does NOT provide Kerberos, Group Policy Objects (GPOs), or Windows machine domain-joining capabilities required by standard legacy Windows applications.

questions.questionText: You are formulating a comprehensive workload disposition framework for an enterprise with 2,000 diverse applications. You are utilizing the standard '6 R's' of migration. Which two application profiles perfectly describe a scenario where the 'Retire' strategy should be selected? (Choose two)
options: An application that provides critical competitive differentiation but runs on an unsupported operating system.
A legacy document management system whose functionality has been fully superseded by a newly deployed Google Workspace environment.
An internal reporting tool that Cloud Migration Center dependency mapping reveals has had zero inbound network connections for the last 12 months.
An application that manages highly classified government data requiring strict air-gapped physical security.
A heavily customized, monolithic ERP system that costs $5 million annually to maintain but is essential for day-to-day operations.
correctAnswers: A legacy document management system whose functionality has been fully superseded by a newly deployed Google Workspace environment.
An internal reporting tool that Cloud Migration Center dependency mapping reveals has had zero inbound network connections for the last 12 months.

explanation.general explanation: The 'Retire' disposition strategy involves decommissioning applications that provide no value to the business, thereby saving infrastructure and licensing costs. This typically applies to: 1) Redundant applications whose functionality has been replaced by newer systems (e.g., moving to Google Workspace renders old document management systems obsolete). 2) 'Zombie' applications that consume resources but are empirically proven (via tools like Migration Center or network logs) to have zero active users or downstream dependencies.

why other options are wrong.An application that provides critical co: Critical applications must be retained or modernized. If the OS is unsupported, it should be Replatformed, Rehosted (e.g., GCVE), or Refactored, but never Retired.
why other options are wrong.An application that manages highly class: This is a textbook case for the 'Retain' strategy (keeping it on-premises or moving it to a specialized air-gapped environment), not retiring it.
why other options are wrong.A heavily customized, monolithic ERP sys: Because it is essential for day-to-day operations, it cannot be retired. It should be evaluated for Refactoring or Repurchasing to reduce the $5M maintenance cost.

questions.questionText: Your team is assessing an on-premises batch processing architecture. The system consists of a clustered file system (Lustre) that ingests massive logs, and an array of 50 compute nodes that run a custom C++ application to parse the logs. The codebase is heavily optimized for POSIX file system APIs. The business wants to migrate to Google Cloud to take advantage of elastic scaling but does not have the budget or C++ expertise to rewrite the application to use object storage APIs (like GCS). What disposition architecture is best?
options: Replatform the architecture by migrating the compute nodes to Compute Engine Managed Instance Groups, and replace the Lustre file system with Cloud Storage, mounting it using Cloud Storage FUSE.
Refactor the architecture by writing a Python wrapper to execute the C++ binary inside Cloud Run, pulling data directly from Cloud Storage.
Replatform the architecture by migrating the compute nodes to Compute Engine Managed Instance Groups, and replace the on-premises Lustre file system with Google Cloud Filestore High Scale.
Rehost the architecture by lifting and shifting the compute nodes to Compute Engine, and building a new Lustre file system on Google Cloud using Persistent Disks attached to VMs.
correctAnswers: Replatform the architecture by migrating the compute nodes to Compute Engine Managed Instance Groups, and replace the on-premises Lustre file system with Google Cloud Filestore High Scale.

explanation.general explanation: The constraints are clear: no budget/expertise to rewrite C++ code, meaning the application absolutely must interact with a high-performance POSIX file system. Google Cloud Filestore High Scale is a managed, highly scalable NAS solution designed specifically for high-performance computing (HPC) and batch processing requiring POSIX compliance. By moving the compute to MIGs (for elasticity) and the storage to Filestore (for managed POSIX performance), you successfully Replatform the workload, achieving cloud benefits without a code rewrite.

why other options are wrong.Replatform the architecture by migrating: Cloud Storage FUSE does not support full POSIX semantics and its performance is vastly inferior to a true clustered file system, making it inappropriate for heavily optimized high-performance batch processing.
why other options are wrong.Refactor the architecture by writing a P: Cloud Run does not provide a native, shared, high-performance distributed file system across instances. The prompt also explicitly bans refactoring to object storage APIs.
why other options are wrong.Rehost the architecture by lifting and s: While building your own Lustre cluster on GCP is possible (Rehosting), it introduces massive operational overhead. Replatforming to a managed service like Filestore High Scale provides the required performance with significantly less management burden.

questions.questionText: You are designing the disposition strategy for an internal corporate communication platform. The platform is a custom-built Ruby on Rails monolithic application. It has low usage, frequent downtime due to memory leaks in the legacy code, and the original developers have left the company. The business requirement is to provide a reliable, feature-rich chat, video, and collaboration tool for employees with zero ongoing IT maintenance. Which disposition strategy is the most optimal?
options: Refactor the Ruby on Rails monolith into serverless Cloud Functions to isolate the memory leaks and ensure high availability.
Replatform the application to App Engine Standard environment, as it fully manages the infrastructure and scales automatically.
Repurchase by migrating the user base to a managed SaaS platform like Google Workspace (Chat/Meet) and decommissioning the legacy Ruby application.
Rehost the application to Compute Engine and implement a robust Cloud Monitoring health check that automatically reboots the VMs when memory leaks occur.
correctAnswers: Repurchase by migrating the user base to a managed SaaS platform like Google Workspace (Chat/Meet) and decommissioning the legacy Ruby application.

explanation.general explanation: The 'Repurchase' (Drop and Shop) strategy is ideal here. Corporate communication (chat/video) is a commodity capability that provides no competitive business differentiation. The custom app is unstable, unmaintained (developers left), and the business wants 'zero ongoing IT maintenance'. Moving to a SaaS platform like Google Workspace entirely eliminates the technical debt and operational burden, perfectly satisfying all business requirements.

why other options are wrong.Refactor the Ruby on Rails monolith into: Refactoring an undocumented, unstable monolith without the original developers is an impossibly high-risk project, and it still leaves IT managing custom code.
why other options are wrong.Replatform the application to App Engine: App Engine manages infrastructure, but it does not fix bad code (memory leaks). The application will still crash, resulting in downtime.
why other options are wrong.Rehost the application to Compute Engine: Rebooting servers to fix memory leaks is an operational nightmare, not a modernization strategy. It guarantees a poor user experience and ongoing IT involvement.

questions.questionText: The Helicopter Racing League (HRL) case study involves migrating their video prediction and rendering pipelines. The existing pipeline uses on-premises bare-metal servers to process massive amounts of telemetry and video data. They want to modernize this to leverage Google Cloud's advanced machine learning capabilities (Vertex AI) and highly elastic compute, accelerating their predictive analytics. Which overall disposition strategy aligns with HRL's goals?
options: Rehost the video rendering software to Compute Engine VMs attached to massive Persistent Disks to mimic the on-premises bare-metal environment.
Retain the video processing on-premises for performance, and use Cloud VPN to send summarized text telemetry to Google Cloud.
Refactor the pipeline to ingest telemetry via Pub/Sub, process it with Dataflow, and utilize Vertex AI and elastic cloud-native services for prediction and rendering.
Repurchase a managed sports broadcasting SaaS platform to handle all video rendering and telemetry analysis externally.
correctAnswers: Refactor the pipeline to ingest telemetry via Pub/Sub, process it with Dataflow, and utilize Vertex AI and elastic cloud-native services for prediction and rendering.

explanation.general explanation: In the HRL case study, the explicit business requirement is to 'accelerate their predictive analytics' and leverage advanced ML. You cannot achieve advanced, elastic ML capabilities by simply copying old architecture. Refactoring the pipeline to use cloud-native data streaming (Pub/Sub, Dataflow) and managed AI services (Vertex AI) allows them to achieve the massive scale, predictive power, and elasticity they desire, fundamentally transforming their architecture.

why other options are wrong.Rehost the video rendering software to C: Mimicking the legacy environment via Lift and Shift (Rehosting) completely fails to leverage the advanced ML and elastic capabilities requested in the case study.
why other options are wrong.Retain the video processing on-premises: The case study explicitly states their goal is to migrate to Google Cloud to leverage its scale, not to retain the heavy processing on-premises.
why other options are wrong.Repurchase a managed sports broadcasting: HRL's competitive advantage lies in their custom predictive models and racing telemetry. Repurchasing a generic SaaS platform would strip them of their unique value proposition.

questions.questionText: Your organization is migrating a legacy, open-source content management system (CMS) that currently runs on an Apache web server and a MySQL database on a single on-premises virtual machine. The business wants to improve the availability and security of the CMS during the migration without altering the application code. They have selected a Replatforming strategy. How should you architect the target state in Google Cloud?
options: Migrate the application to App Engine Flexible to manage the Apache server, and export the database to a Cloud Storage bucket.
Use Migrate to Virtual Machines to lift and shift the entire VM to a single Compute Engine instance in Google Cloud.
Containerize the Apache web application and deploy it to Cloud Run. Migrate the MySQL database to a fully managed Cloud SQL for MySQL instance.
Refactor the CMS backend into microservices using Cloud Functions, and migrate the MySQL data to Cloud Firestore.
correctAnswers: Containerize the Apache web application and deploy it to Cloud Run. Migrate the MySQL database to a fully managed Cloud SQL for MySQL instance.

explanation.general explanation: A 'Replatform' strategy involves making minor architectural changes to take advantage of cloud features without fundamentally rewriting the code. Containerizing the web frontend and putting it on Cloud Run provides instant scalability, load balancing, and SSL termination. Moving the database to Cloud SQL provides automated backups, HA, and patching. The application code itself (the CMS logic and SQL queries) remains identical, fulfilling the requirement of improving availability and security without altering code.

why other options are wrong.Use Migrate to Virtual Machines to lift: This is a Rehosting (Lift and Shift) strategy. Moving a single VM with both the web server and database on it does not meaningfully improve availability or security compared to the on-prem state.
why other options are wrong.Refactor the CMS backend into microservi: This is a massive Refactoring strategy. Converting a MySQL relational database to a NoSQL Firestore database requires fundamentally rewriting the entire data access layer of the application, violating the constraint.
why other options are wrong.Migrate the application to App Engine Fl: You cannot run a MySQL relational database workload out of a Cloud Storage bucket. Cloud Storage is for unstructured object data.

questions.questionText: An enterprise is planning the disposition of its data analytics platform. The current on-premises architecture consists of a massive, heavily customized Apache Kafka cluster for real-time event ingestion, coupled with an Apache Spark cluster for complex stream processing. The data engineering team heavily utilizes custom Kafka Connect plugins that interact with legacy internal mainframes. While the business wants to move to fully managed services to reduce operational overhead, the dependency on the custom mainframe plugins is an absolute blocker for replacing Kafka entirely. Which disposition strategy should you execute?
options: Refactor the entire architecture by replacing Kafka with Google Cloud Pub/Sub and replacing Spark with Cloud Dataflow.
Replatform the architecture by migrating the Spark processing to Cloud Dataproc, but Rehost the Kafka cluster on Compute Engine VMs to maintain plugin compatibility.
Repurchase a fully managed streaming analytics SaaS platform and configure the mainframe to push data directly via REST APIs.
Retain the entire analytics platform on-premises indefinitely, as Google Cloud cannot support hybrid streaming architectures.
correctAnswers: Replatform the architecture by migrating the Spark processing to Cloud Dataproc, but Rehost the Kafka cluster on Compute Engine VMs to maintain plugin compatibility.

explanation.general explanation: Workload disposition does not have to be a one-size-fits-all approach for a complex system. Because the custom Kafka Connect plugins (dependent on the mainframe) act as a hard blocker, you cannot easily replace Kafka with Pub/Sub without massive refactoring. Therefore, you Rehost the Kafka cluster (e.g., on GCE or using Confluent Cloud on GCP) to retain compatibility. However, the Spark processing cluster has no such blockers, so you can Replatform it to managed Cloud Dataproc, achieving the business goal of reducing operational overhead where possible.

why other options are wrong.Refactor the entire architecture by repl: The prompt explicitly states 'dependency on the custom mainframe plugins is an absolute blocker for replacing Kafka entirely.' Pub/Sub does not natively run custom Kafka Connect plugins.
why other options are wrong.Repurchase a fully managed streaming ana: Reconfiguring a legacy mainframe to push data via REST APIs is a massive, high-risk refactoring effort that is likely impossible without specialized developers.
why other options are wrong.Retain the entire analytics platform on-: Google Cloud fully supports running Kafka on VMs (or via partners) alongside managed services. Retaining the entire platform ignores the business goal of reducing operational overhead.

questions.questionText: During the discovery and assessment phase of a workload disposition strategy, you utilize Google Cloud Migration Center. You have deployed the discovery client to your on-premises data center. Which two critical data points provided by Migration Center are essential for deciding whether to Rehost, Replatform, or Retire a specific virtual machine? (Choose two)
options: Automated translation of legacy COBOL source code into Java.
Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) comparisons mapping the on-premises VM sizing to right-sized Google Cloud instances.
Network dependency mapping showing inbound and outbound connections to identify tightly coupled application tiers.
Vulnerability scanning results identifying zero-day exploits within the application's proprietary source code.
Automated schema refactoring recommendations for converting NoSQL databases to Cloud Spanner.
correctAnswers: Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) comparisons mapping the on-premises VM sizing to right-sized Google Cloud instances.
Network dependency mapping showing inbound and outbound connections to identify tightly coupled application tiers.

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud Migration Center (formerly StratoZone) is an assessment tool used to drive disposition decisions. Its core capabilities include performance data collection to generate accurate TCO reports (showing how much a VM would cost to Rehost vs. Replatform) based on actual usage, not just provisioned capacity. Crucially, it provides network dependency mapping, which is vital for identifying application groups (what must migrate together) and identifying dead applications that have no connections (candidates for Retire).

why other options are wrong.Automated translation of legacy COBOL so: Migration Center is an infrastructure and dependency assessment tool. It does not inspect, read, or translate application source code.
why other options are wrong.Vulnerability scanning results identifyi: Migration Center gathers infrastructure metadata (CPU, RAM, OS version, network ports). It is not a Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tool.
why other options are wrong.Automated schema refactoring recommendat: While Google offers Database Migration Service for some translations, Migration Center itself does not analyze database schemas or recommend complex NoSQL-to-Spanner refactoring logic.

questions.questionText: Your team is defining the disposition strategy for an internal HR portal. The application is a monolithic LAMP stack (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP) running on a single on-premises VM. The business requires the application to handle high availability and automatic scaling to accommodate annual open-enrollment traffic spikes. They are willing to make minor configuration changes but strictly prohibit rewriting the core PHP application logic. Which strategy should you recommend?
options: Refactor the application by rewriting the PHP code into Node.js and deploying it to Cloud Functions for infinite scalability.
Rehost the VM using Migrate to Virtual Machines, enabling Compute Engine autoscaling based on memory utilization.
Replatform the application by containerizing the Apache/PHP frontend and deploying to Cloud Run, and migrating the MySQL database to Cloud SQL.
Repurchase the HR portal by migrating to a managed SaaS provider, retaining the MySQL database on-premises for compliance.
correctAnswers: Replatform the application by containerizing the Apache/PHP frontend and deploying to Cloud Run, and migrating the MySQL database to Cloud SQL.

explanation.general explanation: The constraints prohibit rewriting core logic (ruling out Refactoring) but require high availability and autoscaling. Replatforming (Lift and Optimize) is the correct approach. Containerizing the LAMP frontend and moving it to Cloud Run allows it to scale from zero to massive capacity automatically during enrollment spikes. Moving the database to Cloud SQL provides high availability and managed backups. This architecture provides cloud-native benefits without altering the underlying PHP application code.

why other options are wrong.Refactor the application by rewriting th: The prompt states: 'strictly prohibit rewriting the core PHP application logic'. This option directly violates that constraint.
why other options are wrong.Rehost the VM using Migrate to Virtual M: While Rehosting moves the VM to the cloud, putting a monolithic application (where the DB and web server share the same disk) into an autoscaling group will result in data corruption, as multiple instances will try to write to separate local databases. The state (DB) must be decoupled.
why other options are wrong.Repurchase the HR portal by migrating to: Moving to a SaaS provider implies using their backend. You typically cannot use a modern SaaS product while keeping its core relational database locked on-premises.

questions.questionText: An enterprise is planning its workload disposition strategy for a massive, heavily customized ERP system. The migration assessment reveals that the ERP database communicates with 45 peripheral applications (reporting engines, billing systems, logistics APIs) located both on-premises and in other public clouds. Which two factors are the most critical technical constraints to evaluate when deciding whether to 'Rehost' this ERP system to Google Cloud in the first migration wave? (Choose two)
options: Network latency and bandwidth capacity between Google Cloud and the on-premises/multi-cloud peripheral applications.
The availability of equivalent managed PaaS offerings (like Cloud SQL) in Google Cloud.
The potential data egress costs generated by the ERP database continuously synchronizing with the peripheral applications.
The ability of Google Cloud Identity to federate with the legacy ERP's local user repository.
The programming languages used to develop the 45 peripheral applications.
correctAnswers: Network latency and bandwidth capacity between Google Cloud and the on-premises/multi-cloud peripheral applications.
The potential data egress costs generated by the ERP database continuously synchronizing with the peripheral applications.

explanation.general explanation: When Rehosting a heavily coupled 'center of gravity' application like an ERP system while leaving its dependencies behind (split-stack architecture), physics and economics are the primary constraints. 1) Network Latency/Bandwidth: If the ERP is in GCP and 45 apps on-prem rely on sub-millisecond database queries, the application will break due to the speed of light. 2) Egress Costs: Data flowing out of Google Cloud back to on-prem or AWS incurs network egress fees. A highly chatty ERP database could generate massive, unexpected cloud bills.

why other options are wrong.The availability of equivalent managed P: The strategy selected is 'Rehost' (Lift and Shift to VMs). Therefore, managed PaaS availability is irrelevant, as the database will run on IaaS VMs.
why other options are wrong.The ability of Google Cloud Identity to: While identity is important, an ERP system's core technical viability during migration is dictated by its network dependencies. Local authentication works exactly the same on a VM in GCP as it does on-premises.
why other options are wrong.The programming languages used to develo: The programming languages of downstream applications are irrelevant to the network communication layer (e.g., TCP/IP, JDBC, HTTP) connecting them to the ERP database.

questions.questionText: Your company decides to Refactor a legacy, on-premises monolithic application into a microservices architecture on Google Cloud. The legacy application relies heavily on a local file system to store temporary session states and intermediate processing files. To ensure the new microservices running on Cloud Run are truly cloud-native and resilient, how should you alter the application's interaction with the file system during the refactoring process?
options: Refactor the code to utilize the Cloud Run local in-memory file system (`/tmp`) for persistent session storage across container reboots.
Refactor the microservices to externalize all state, utilizing Memorystore for session data and Cloud Storage for intermediate file processing.
Mount a Google Cloud Filestore instance to the Cloud Run services to mimic the persistent local file system of the legacy monolith.
Package the legacy local file system into the Docker container image so the microservices have continuous access to the historical data.
correctAnswers: Refactor the microservices to externalize all state, utilizing Memorystore for session data and Cloud Storage for intermediate file processing.

explanation.general explanation: A fundamental principle of Refactoring to cloud-native microservices (especially serverless like Cloud Run) is that compute instances must be stateless. Relying on local file systems for state violates the Twelve-Factor App methodology. The correct disposition architecture requires externalizing the state. Session state, which requires low-latency read/writes, should be moved to an in-memory datastore like Memorystore (Redis). Intermediate files should be streamed to object storage like Cloud Storage. This allows Cloud Run to scale out infinitely without data loss or corruption.

why other options are wrong.Refactor the code to utilize the Cloud R: The `/tmp` directory in Cloud Run is strictly an in-memory ramdisk. It is ephemeral. If the container spins down or scales out, the data is lost immediately. It cannot be used for 'persistent' session storage.
why other options are wrong.Mount a Google Cloud Filestore instance: While Cloud Run supports network file systems, mimicking a monolithic local file system across distributed microservices often introduces massive locking and concurrency bottlenecks, defeating the purpose of refactoring.
why other options are wrong.Package the legacy local file system int: Docker images are immutable. You cannot write dynamic session state back into the underlying container image during runtime.

questions.questionText: A logistics company uses an on-premises architecture where warehouse scanners push inventory update files via FTP to a central Linux server. A cron job on the server runs every 5 minutes, executing a Python script that parses the files and updates a local database. The company wants to completely Refactor this event-driven workflow to an entirely serverless, NoOps architecture in Google Cloud. Which combination of GCP services should they adopt for the new architecture? (Choose two)
options: Use Cloud Storage to receive the inventory files from the scanners.
Use a Compute Engine Managed Instance Group running an FTP server to receive the files.
Configure Cloud Storage to emit Eventarc triggers to a Cloud Function that parses the file upon upload.
Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Dataproc cluster every 5 minutes to parse the files.
Store the parsed inventory data in a persistent local disk attached to the Cloud Function.
correctAnswers: Use Cloud Storage to receive the inventory files from the scanners.
Configure Cloud Storage to emit Eventarc triggers to a Cloud Function that parses the file upon upload.

explanation.general explanation: To achieve a fully serverless, Refactored, event-driven architecture, you must replace the legacy components (FTP, Cron, persistent VMs). 1) Cloud Storage replaces the FTP server; scanners can upload files directly to a bucket via signed URLs or API. 2) Eventarc replaces the 5-minute Cron job. When a file lands in the bucket, an event is instantly emitted, triggering a serverless Cloud Function. The Cloud Function executes the Python parsing logic and updates a managed database (like Firestore or Cloud SQL), resulting in zero infrastructure to manage (NoOps).

why other options are wrong.Use a Compute Engine Managed Instance Gr: Compute Engine VMs are Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS), not serverless. This represents a Rehost strategy, not the requested Refactor to serverless.
why other options are wrong.Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Datapro: While Dataproc is powerful, spinning up a Hadoop/Spark cluster every 5 minutes to parse simple scanner files is massive overkill, highly inefficient, and not truly serverless compared to Cloud Functions.
why other options are wrong.Store the parsed inventory data in a per: Cloud Functions are stateless and ephemeral; you cannot attach persistent local disks to them for long-term database storage.
